Unlike spoken languages that are linear and auditory, sign languages are visual and spatial, conveying meaning through a rich articulation of manual components—handshape, orientation, location, and movement—synchronized with non-manual signals like facial expressions and body posture \cite{valli2000linguistics}. Capturing this intricate grammar and semantic nuance requires sensing technologies capable of exceptional fidelity and temporal resolution. Consequently, developing a system that is both linguistically accurate and universally accessible represents a grand challenge in the field \cite{wen2021ai, zhou2020sign}.

Concurrently, computer vision has been the dominant paradigm addressing this challenge \cite{rastgoo2021sign}. Leveraging the ubiquity of RGB cameras and deep neural networks, state-of-the-art models can now reconstruct intricate 3D hand poses with high fidelity \cite{pavlakos2024reconstructing, lugaresi2019mediapipe}. However, the reliance on optical sensors creates a fundamental conflict between technological capability and user privacy. The deployment of cameras in personal spaces, such as bedrooms, bathrooms, or medical settings, inherently raises significant concerns, a topic of growing scrutiny in the age of ubiquitous AI \cite{ryoo2017privacy}. Furthermore, optical systems are susceptible to environmental constraints like poor lighting or visual clutter, rendering them unreliable for the very real-world scenarios where assistance is most needed. This necessitates a shift toward alternative modalities that can ensure both privacy and robustness without compromising linguistic understanding \cite{zhang2024monitoring, zhuang2025advancing}.

To overcome the limitations of vision-based systems, researchers have explored alternative modalities. Wearable devices capture precise flexion but impose an intrusive physical burden that precludes ubiquitous adoption. In contrast, radio-frequency (RF) sensing, particularly millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, has emerged as a compelling privacy-preserving alternative. However, the current landscape of RF-based sign language analysis remains fundamentally bifurcated. One stream focuses exclusively on closed-set classification, recognizing only predefined vocabularies of isolated gestures. These approaches inherently fail to scale to the combinatorial complexity of open-vocabulary communication. The other stream targets kinematic reconstruction, recovering hand geometry without extracting linguistic meaning. Consequently, a critical disconnect persists: while existing methods can either classify a limited lexicon or reconstruct geometric shapes, no framework has yet established a unified pathway that bridges the gap from raw physical signals to high-level semantic interpretation. This disconnection stems from the ill-posed nature of mapping sparse and specular radar echoes directly to complex linguistic structures \cite{wagih2024wide, pistore2021millimeter, zhang2024monitoring}.

all.caption: \textbf{Schematic of the mmPRISM framework for privacy-preserving continuous sign language understanding.} \textbf{a} MmWave radar serves as the core sensing module capturing hand gesture dynamics, anchoring the pipeline, bridging raw mmWave signals and linguistic interpretation to enable robust communication for Deaf and hard-of-hearing communities without visually identifiable data. \textbf{b} Hand reconstruction network: Raw radar data is processed into a range-Doppler-azimuth-elevation tensor preserving spatial and velocity information, as the foundational input for generating high-fidelity two-hand skeletal poses (mmw-pose). \textbf{c} Sign language understanding LLM: An mT5-based encoder-decoder model integrated with confidence-aware multi-modal fusion—fusing STGCN-extracted pose and raw mmWave features to mitigate self-occlusion—for structured semantic processing. \textbf{d} Hand reconstruction evaluation: Quantitative comparison with the mmHand baseline in the near-field (<0.5 m), where mmPRISM achieves 15 mm MPJPE and 98\% 3D-PCK, significantly outperforming the baseline. \textbf{e} Semantic interpretation: The LLM generates coherent natural language outputs supporting both isolated gestures (e.g., “morning”) and complex sentences (e.g., “Good morning, please help me draft a reply to this email”).

\textbf{Architecture of the volumetric feature extraction module.} The system processes the 4D RF tensor through a hierarchical backbone to extract discriminative spatial features. \textbf{(a)} A multi-attention mechanism synergistically combines spatial, channel, and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules to highlight salient geometric structures while adaptively suppressing multipath noise. \textbf{(b)} The fundamental processing unit, utilizing efficient convolutional operations to preserve local spatial context. \textbf{(c)} The overall encoder backbone, incorporating a path aggregation feature pyramid to fuse features across different scales. This design preserves both the fine-grained details essential for finger tracking and the high-level contextual information required for global pose inference.

all.caption: \textbf{Temporal aggregation for dynamic consistency.} Following frame-wise spatial feature extraction by CubeNet, the sequential features are processed by a hybrid temporal transformer to model gesture dynamics. Equipped with Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), the transformer captures short-range and long-range temporal dependencies, while multi-strategy aggregation (CLS token, mean pooling, attention pooling) fuses sequence features via learnable weighted fusion. Operating in a sliding-window manner, this module resolves kinematic ambiguities from self-occlusion or sparse mmWave signals, yielding temporally coherent and anatomically plausible two-hand pose estimates (mmw-pose).

all.caption: \textbf{Robustness of kinematic reconstruction across operational regimes.} Quantitative benchmarks compare mmPRISM with the mmHand baseline across three distance ranges: near-field (<0.5\,m), mid-range ($\approx 1$\,m), and far-field (>2\,m). Our geometry-guided approach maintains superior performance consistently, achieving 15\,mm MPJPE and 98\% 3D-PCK in the near-field, while retaining <35\,mm error in the far-field. In contrast, the baseline suffers sharp accuracy degradation under far-field signal sparsity, highlighting mmPRISM's robustness for practical deployment.

all.caption: \textbf{Visual validation of structural integrity for hand pose reconstruction.} Qualitative comparison includes RGB reference images, ground-truth skeletal poses, mmPRISM outputs, and mmHand baseline results. Our framework maintains anatomical integrity and distinct fine-grained finger separation even during complex sign language articulations (e.g., dexterous finger flexion and inter-hand interaction), whereas the mmHand baseline frequently suffers from digit merging, joint misalignment, or structural collapse. This superior structural preservation ensures the capture of fine-grained motion cues that are critical for accurate downstream sign language understanding.

all.caption: \textbf{Domain adaptation via shallow-layer alignment.} To mitigate the statistical discrepancy between physics-based synthetic mmWave data (generated via MANO model and ray-tracing) and real-world sensor signals, we freeze the semantic-rich deep layers of CubeNet (stage layers and MLP decoder) while fine-tuning only the initial stem layers. This strategy adapts to low-level signal statistics of real data, mapping diverse inputs into a shared domain-invariant feature space, validated by t-SNE visualization—facilitating robust generalization of mmw-pose reconstruction.

To resolve this, we introduce a targeted feature alignment strategy (Fig.~\ref{fig:training}). Hypothesizing that the domain discrepancy is primarily encoded in low-level signal statistics rather than high-level semantic structures, we freeze the deeper task-oriented layers of the feature extractor and fine-tune only the initial stem layers on a small set of real-world data. This strategy effectively repurposes the stem layers to function as a learnable sensor calibrator that harmonizes signal statistics, while the frozen deep layers preserve the universal kinematic priors acquired from large-scale simulation. To ensure robust translation, the system employs a confidence-aware fusion mechanism (Fig.~\ref{fig:llm}) that treats the reconstructed skeleton and raw radar features as synergistic rather than redundant. While the skeletal stream provides explicit topological structure, the raw radar stream preserves subtle micro-dynamics and environmental context often filtered out during reconstruction. Consequently, the adaptive gating does not merely act as a fallback for tracking errors; instead, it dynamically synthesizes these modalities, leveraging the raw signal's rich density to compensate for geometric uncertainty during severe occlusions, thereby maintaining a continuous and holistic semantic flow.

This resilient feature stream is then processed by an encoder-decoder LLM trained via a progressive curriculum (Fig.~\ref{fig:llm}b). Recognizing the modality gap between visual training data and RF inference data, we structured the learning process into three stages: \textit{Foundational Semantic Learning} where the model learns linguistic structures from clean camera-based poses; Cross-modal Adaptation where it adapts to the noise patterns of our synthetic RF poses; and Real-world Calibration which is a final fine-tuning phase on limited real sensor data.

We benchmarked this system against three representative baselines: an end-to-end model processing raw radar cubes, a heatmap-based 2D encoder, and a point-cloud-based architecture (Table~\ref{tab:llm_results}). Our approach achieves a BLEU-4 score of 15.82 and more than doubles the performance of the nearest competitor. Crucially, it recovers over 84\% of the translation quality of a vision-based oracle system. This demonstrates that our physics-informed reconstruction and domain adaptation strategies have effectively closed the gap between RF sensing and optical perception.

all.caption: \textbf{4D mmWave Cube for geometry-guided hand pose reconstruction.} This visualization illustrates the core volumetric data structure of mmPRISM, constructed via physics-informed signal processing of raw millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar echoes. The cube encapsulates four dimensions: Doppler (velocity, $N_D$), range (distance, $N_R$), azimuth (horizontal angle, $N_{azi}$), and elevation (vertical angle, $N_{ele}$), fully preserving 3D spatial context and motion dynamics critical for fine-grained hand articulation capture. For intuitive interpretation, annotations are colored according to the velocity corresponding to the maximum energy value of the Doppler vector, distinguishing dynamic hand movements (left hand, right hand) from static body regions and environmental clutter. Unlike conventional methods that rely on dimensionality-reduced projections or sparse point clouds, this 4D representation maximizes information retention, laying the foundation for CubeNet to extract discriminative spatial features and resolve ambiguities in sparse radar signals. The data structure is generated through a two-step process: first, 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of raw ADC data to extract range-Doppler information, followed by beamforming imaging to map spatial angles, with static clutter removed by subtracting the DC component to enhance signal-to-noise ratio for dynamic hand targets. This physics-grounded design ensures the preservation of fine-grained motion cues essential for accurate mmw-pose reconstruction and downstream sign language understanding.

The right subplot (after alignment) demonstrates significant intermingling of the two feature clusters, confirming that our targeted transfer learning approach—freezing semantic-rich deep layers of CubeNet while fine-tuning only initial stem layers—successfully harmonizes the statistical distributions. This alignment ensures that high-level kinematic knowledge learned from large-scale synthetic data (leveraging abundant sign language video corpora) can be reliably transferred to real-world scenarios, enabling consistent mmw-pose reconstruction performance across both data sources. captions: \textbf{Comparison of temporal aggregation methods for geometry-guided hand pose reconstruction.} This table quantifies the performance of different temporal modeling strategies in capturing spatio-temporal dynamics of hand gestures, a critical step for high-fidelity mmw-pose reconstruction. captions: \textbf{Performance of mmPRISM on generalization tests for geometry-guided sign language understanding.} This table quantifies the robustness of mmPRISM’s hand pose reconstruction module across three critical generalization scenarios, evaluating its ability to adapt to unseen conditions— a key requirement for practical deployment. The tested scenarios include: (1) Cross-Temporal (random splits over the full dataset, serving as the baseline), (2) Cross-Individual (leave-one-participant-out protocol, training on all subjects except one to test user-agnostic feature learning), and (3) Cross-Environment (training in the primary ideal collection space and testing in a distinct room with different geometry and materials to assess environmental adaptability). Two core metrics are reported: Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE, lower values indicate higher accuracy) and 3D Percentage of Correct Keypoints (3D-PCK, higher values indicate more reliable joint localization). Results show that mmPRISM maintains stable performance across all scenarios: Cross-Temporal (MPJPE: 23.23 mm, 3D-PCK: 96.62\%), Cross-Individual (MPJPE: 26.42 mm, 3D-PCK: 95.45\%), and Cross-Environment (MPJPE: 25.89 mm, 3D-PCK: 95.71\%). The modest performance gap relative to the baseline confirms that the model learns identity-invariant hand pose features (rather than overfitting to specific anatomies or motion styles) and can reliably transfer to previously unseen environments. This generalization capability underscores mmPRISM’s practical utility for real-world sign language interaction, where users and environments are often unpredictable.

captions: \textbf{4D mmWave Cube for geometry-guided hand pose reconstruction.} This visualization illustrates the core volumetric data structure of mmPRISM, constructed via physics-informed signal processing of raw millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar echoes. The cube encapsulates four dimensions: Doppler (velocity, $N_D$), range (distance, $N_R$), azimuth (horizontal angle, $N_{azi}$), and elevation (vertical angle, $N_{ele}$), fully preserving 3D spatial context and motion dynamics critical for fine-grained hand articulation capture. For intuitive interpretation, annotations are colored according to the velocity corresponding to the maximum energy value of the Doppler vector, distinguishing dynamic hand movements (left hand, right hand) from static body regions and environmental clutter. Unlike conventional methods that rely on dimensionality-reduced projections or sparse point clouds, this 4D representation maximizes information retention, laying the foundation for CubeNet to extract discriminative spatial features and resolve ambiguities in sparse radar signals. The data structure is generated through a two-step process: first, 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of raw ADC data to extract range-Doppler information, followed by beamforming imaging to map spatial angles, with static clutter removed by subtracting the DC component to enhance signal-to-noise ratio for dynamic hand targets. This physics-grounded design ensures the preservation of fine-grained motion cues essential for accurate mmw-pose reconstruction and downstream sign language understanding.

captions: \textbf{Performance of mmPRISM on generalization tests for geometry-guided sign language understanding.} This table quantifies the robustness of mmPRISM’s hand pose reconstruction module across three critical generalization scenarios, evaluating its ability to adapt to unseen conditions— a key requirement for practical deployment. The tested scenarios include: (1) Cross-Temporal (random splits over the full dataset, serving as the baseline), (2) Cross-Individual (leave-one-participant-out protocol, training on all subjects except one to test user-agnostic feature learning), and (3) Cross-Environment (training in the primary ideal collection space and testing in a distinct room with different geometry and materials to assess environmental adaptability). Two core metrics are reported: Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE, lower values indicate higher accuracy) and 3D Percentage of Correct Keypoints (3D-PCK, higher values indicate more reliable joint localization). Results show that mmPRISM maintains stable performance across all scenarios: Cross-Temporal (MPJPE: 23.23 mm, 3D-PCK: 96.62\%), Cross-Individual (MPJPE: 26.42 mm, 3D-PCK: 95.45\%), and Cross-Environment (MPJPE: 25.89 mm, 3D-PCK: 95.71\%). The modest performance gap relative to the baseline confirms that the model learns identity-invariant hand pose features (rather than overfitting to specific anatomies or motion styles) and can reliably transfer to previously unseen environments. This generalization capability underscores mmPRISM’s practical utility for real-world sign language interaction, where users and environments are often unpredictable.

captions: \textbf{Performance of mmPRISM’s hand pose reconstruction under real-world noisy scenarios.} This table quantifies the robustness of the geometry-guided mmw-pose reconstruction module in challenging environmental conditions, a key advantage of mmWave-based sensing over vision-based systems. Two core metrics are reported: Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE, lower values indicate higher accuracy) and 3D Percentage of Correct Keypoints (3D-PCK, higher values indicate more reliable joint localization). Results show that mmPRISM maintains stable performance across all noisy scenarios: Poor-light (MPJPE: 23.47 mm, 3D-PCK: 96.48\%), Multi-person (MPJPE: 27.51 mm, 3D-PCK: 95.14\%), Reflector (MPJPE: 25.56 mm, 3D-PCK: 96.34\%), with only modest degradation compared to the ideal setting (MPJPE: 23.23 mm, 3D-PCK: 96.62\%). This validates the system’s inherent resilience to environmental stressors, enabled by physics-informed signal processing and robust feature extraction, ensuring reliable hand pose reconstruction for sign language understanding in real-world, unconstrained environments.
